title: Strider
summary: Strider, also reported as ProjectSauron, is a long-running espionage operation described in public reporting as unusually selective. Instead of broad phishing at scale, it was observed compromising a very small number of government, military, financial and telecommunications organisations across several countries. Its framework was modular and stealth-oriented: operators deployed components only on hosts they judged interesting, used hidden storage inside the file system, and included features intended to survive removal attempts. That combination means defenders rarely see commodity malware files, and detection usually depends on network anomalies, unexpected scheduled tasks, unusual service configuration and careful host forensics. Two misunderstandings persist: that a serious intrusion must leave obvious malicious binaries behind, and that stealth equals invulnerability. Public reporting discusses the operation's possible sponsorship but does not present it as a settled finding, so any attribution should be quoted with the confidence its source uses.

beginner.definition: Strider is a name for an espionage group that is very careful and very patient. Public reports describe it as attacking only a few chosen organisations instead of millions of people at once. It hides its tools deep inside the computer, so a simple cleanup may miss them. Researchers also call the same activity ProjectSauron.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most attackers are noisy and get caught quickly. This one is quiet, so ordinary antivirus alerts may never appear. If your organisation holds sensitive research, financial records or government material, an intrusion of this kind can stay in place for years. The longer an attacker stays, the more they learn and copy. Understanding this style of attack helps you look for small signs instead of waiting for a loud alarm.
howItWorks: The group selects a very small set of targets after studying them for a long period.
Access often begins with a stolen password, a weak remote service or a compromised trusted partner.
Once inside, the operators place a small loader that hides in a legitimate-looking system location.
Extra tools are deployed only to machines that seem worth reading, which keeps noise low.
Stolen files leave through normal network paths, so the traffic resembles everyday business activity.
Some components survive cleanup, which allows the group to return without breaking in again.
beginner.example: Think of a large public library. A thief does not steal the whole building. They borrow a membership card, sit in a quiet corner, and photocopy one page a day for a year. The staff notice nothing unusual, because reading books is normal there. Strider works the same way. It uses the roads your organisation already uses, takes small amounts of data at a time, and leaves a spare key hidden between the shelves.
takeaways: Quiet intrusions often hide inside normal administration activity.
Removing visible malware is not the same as removing the attacker.
Small unusual network patterns matter more than large obvious alarms.

objectives: Explain what makes Strider an unusually selective espionage operation.
Describe how a modular framework reduces the noise an intruder creates.
Identify host and network evidence that suggests long-term hidden access.
Explain why public attribution for this group stays deliberately cautious.
Summarise why full remediation is harder than deleting a malicious file.
